A brief note on why Generative AI earns a dedicated module in Artificial Intelligence. At this level, coursework is structured so that each topic does real conceptual work -- it either resolves a limitation of the previous topic, extends it to a broader class of cases, or introduces a method that later topics reuse. Understanding which of these roles Generative AI plays will make the rest of the module easier to follow.

The intended learning outcomes for this module are: Explain the core ideas of generative ai at Undergraduate Year 4 depth; Apply generative ai concepts to worked examples and problems; Critically discuss how generative ai connects to real-world practice in artificial intelligence. Treat these less as a checklist and more as a self-assessment tool: after working through the material, try to satisfy each outcome without reference to your notes, and any outcome you cannot satisfy cleanly marks exactly where to focus your remaining study time.

Central terminology for this module: Generative. A useful habit at this stage of study is to maintain your own running glossary rather than relying on recognising terms in context; being asked to produce a definition cold, without the surrounding sentence to lean on, is a much better test of whether a concept has actually been internalised.

Students frequently underestimate how much of the difficulty in material like this is conceptual rather than computational: getting the right numeric answer to a problem is not the same as being able to explain, in your own words and without notes, why the method used was appropriate. Assessment at this level increasingly rewards the latter, so it is worth practising explanation, not just calculation, as you work through the material.

To consolidate this module, work through the following: Guided worked example on generative ai; Small-group discussion / problem set on generative ai. Treat this as a diagnostic as much as an exercise: wherever it exposes a gap in your understanding, that gap is exactly where additional study time is best spent, rather than spreading review evenly across material you have already mastered.

The associated assignment is: Write a short summary connecting generative ai to one real-world example. To close, treat mastery of Generative AI as an ongoing project rather than a one-time task completed when the module ends. Design a mini-project applying 'Behavioral Economics' to a real dataset, case, or scenario relevant to economics.
Prepare a undergraduate year 4 presentation comparing two modules covered in this level of Economics.
real_world_examples: How 'Exchange Rates & the Balance of Payments' shows up in real-world economics practice: How currencies are valued and how international accounts balance.
How 'Behavioral Economics' shows up in real-world economics practice: How real human decision-making departs from purely rational models.

How 'Mechanism Design' shows up in real-world economics practice: Studies how to design rules and institutions that achieve desired outcomes when participants hold private information, including incentive compatibility and the revelation principle.

How 'Institutional Economics' shows up in real-world economics practice: Examines how property rights, contracts, and political institutions shape transaction costs and long-run economic performance, drawing on the work of Coase and North.

Learners should complete modules in order, attempt the quiz after each module, and take the level exam once all modules are complete before advancing to the next level.

learning_objectives: Explain the core ideas of philosophy of mind at Undergraduate Year 4 depth.

lessons.reading_material:
Consciousness, the mind-body problem, and personal identity.

Philosophy of Mind sits at a point in Philosophy where genuine understanding pays off disproportionately: it is referenced, directly or indirectly, in a wide range of subsequent material. Students who treat it as a box to check tend to find themselves relearning it under time pressure later; students who invest in understanding it now tend to find later modules noticeably more tractable.

The intended learning outcomes for this module are: Explain the core ideas of philosophy of mind at Undergraduate Year 4 depth; Apply philosophy of mind concepts to worked examples and problems; Critically discuss how philosophy of mind connects to real-world practice in philosophy. Treat these less as a checklist and more as a self-assessment tool: after working through the material, try to satisfy each outcome without reference to your notes, and any outcome you cannot satisfy cleanly marks exactly where to focus your remaining study time.

Central terminology for this module: Philosophy, Mind. A useful habit at this stage of study is to maintain your own running glossary rather than relying on recognising terms in context; being asked to produce a definition cold, without the surrounding sentence to lean on, is a much better test of whether a concept has actually been internalised.

Students frequently underestimate how much of the difficulty in material like this is conceptual rather than computational: getting the right numeric answer to a problem is not the same as being able to explain, in your own words and without notes, why the method used was appropriate. Assessment at this level increasingly rewards the latter, so it is worth practising explanation, not just calculation, as you work through the material.

Capstone Study: Art History is a capstone-level undergraduate module in Art, deepening prior levels with more rigorous theory, worked examples, and assessment matched to Undergraduate Year 4.

A brief note on why Capstone Study: Art History earns a dedicated module in Art. At this level, coursework is structured so that each topic does real conceptual work -- it either resolves a limitation of the previous topic, extends it to a broader class of cases, or introduces a method that later topics reuse. Understanding which of these roles Capstone Study: Art History plays will make the rest of the module easier to follow.

The intended learning outcomes for this module are: Explain the core ideas of capstone study: art history at Undergraduate Year 4 depth; Apply capstone study: art history concepts to worked examples and problems; Critically discuss how capstone study: art history connects to real-world practice in art. Treat these less as a checklist and more as a self-assessment tool: after working through the material, try to satisfy each outcome without reference to your notes, and any outcome you cannot satisfy cleanly marks exactly where to focus your remaining study time.

Central terminology for this module: Capstone, Study, History. A useful habit at this stage of study is to maintain your own running glossary rather than relying on recognising terms in context; being asked to produce a definition cold, without the surrounding sentence to lean on, is a much better test of whether a concept has actually been internalised.

lessons.reading_material:
Capstone Study: Cognitive Bias & Fallacies is a capstone-level undergraduate module in Critical Thinking, deepening prior levels with more rigorous theory, worked examples, and assessment matched to Undergraduate Year 4.

Capstone Study: Cognitive Bias & Fallacies sits at a point in Critical Thinking where genuine understanding pays off disproportionately: it is referenced, directly or indirectly, in a wide range of subsequent material. Students who treat it as a box to check tend to find themselves relearning it under time pressure later; students who invest in understanding it now tend to find later modules noticeably more tractable.

The intended learning outcomes for this module are: Explain the core ideas of capstone study: cognitive bias & fallacies at Undergraduate Year 4 depth; Apply capstone study: cognitive bias & fallacies concepts to worked examples and problems; Critically discuss how capstone study: cognitive bias & fallacies connects to real-world practice in critical thinking. Treat these less as a checklist and more as a self-assessment tool: after working through the material, try to satisfy each outcome without reference to your notes, and any outcome you cannot satisfy cleanly marks exactly where to focus your remaining study time.

Central terminology for this module: Capstone, Study, Cognitive, Bias, Fallacies. A useful habit at this stage of study is to maintain your own running glossary rather than relying on recognising terms in context; being asked to produce a definition cold, without the surrounding sentence to lean on, is a much better test of whether a concept has actually been internalised.

Students frequently underestimate how much of the difficulty in material like this is conceptual rather than computational: getting the right numeric answer to a problem is not the same as being able to explain, in your own words and without notes, why the method used was appropriate. Assessment at this level increasingly rewards the latter, so it is worth practising explanation, not just calculation, as you work through the material.

To consolidate this module, work through the following: Guided worked example on capstone study: cognitive bias & fallacies; Small-group discussion / problem set on capstone study: cognitive bias & fallacies. Treat this as a diagnostic as much as an exercise: wherever it exposes a gap in your understanding, that gap is exactly where additional study time is best spent, rather than spreading review evenly across material you have already mastered.

The associated assignment is: Write a short summary connecting capstone study: cognitive bias & fallacies to one real-world example. Beyond satisfying the requirement, use it as an opportunity to surface exactly which parts of the module you can apply confidently and which parts you can only recognise -- that distinction is the most useful information you can extract from any assignment.

For review before assessment: Review capstone study: cognitive bias & fallacies before moving to the next module. A strong test of readiness is being able to reconstruct the core argument of this module from a blank page, in your own words and without consulting notes; if you can do that fluently, recognition-based review is no longer the most valuable use of your remaining study time.

To close, treat mastery of Capstone Study: Cognitive Bias & Fallacies as an ongoing project rather than a one-time task completed when the module ends. Topics at this level are rarely self-contained; Capstone Study: Cognitive Bias & Fallacies both depends on concepts introduced earlier in the course and sets up reasoning that later modules will assume you already have available. Treating it as an isolated fact to memorise, rather than a piece of a larger argument, is the single most common reason students find later material harder than it needs to be.
